# Conclusions

Schools socialize students into beliefs about meritocracy, promoting effort and talent as the legitimate basis of reward while simultaneously exposing them to the weight of family resources and social connections in shaping outcomes [@resh_sense_2014; @traini_stratification_2022; @goudeau_hidden_2017a]. Many students navigate this tension by holding both orientations at once, endorsing merit as an ideal while recognizing that privilege structures actual outcomes, a configuration that can be associated with _dual consciousness_ [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025; @kluegel_beliefs_1987]. Extending Castillo et al.'s [-@castillo_multidimensional_2023] multidimensional framework to two cohorts of Chilean students (6th and 9th graders in 2023, followed into 7th and 10th grade in 2024), the measurement of meritocratic and privilege beliefs provides evidence of reliability in school-aged populations, and equivalently over time. This is a foundational contribution: a precondition for studying the developmental trajectory of meritocratic beliefs and their educational implications, such as gender and social class differences.

This study draws on a non-probability sample of nine schools in one country, so its results cannot be statistically generalized, but three of its contributions may be relevant beyond this setting. First, the distinctions between perceived and preferred meritocracy, and between meritocratic and privilege-based principles, may reflect cognitive and normative capacities that develop during adolescence, although whether the four-factor structure replicates in other societies remains to be established. Second, the coexistence of merit endorsement and recognition of privilege has been documented in China [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025], the United States and Finland [@zhu_meritocratic_2025], and Europe [@kwon_multidimensionality_2024], suggesting it is not a Chilean peculiarity. Third, longitudinal invariance testing as a prerequisite for developmental inference applies to any panel study of meritocratic beliefs. By contrast, the cross-cohort non-invariance may be more system-dependent, reflecting the intensity and timing of school-based sorting in Chile's tracked and marketized system [@madariaga_three_2020; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2013]; research in countries with different tracking regimes will help clarify which aspects of measurement equivalence are universal.

This study has limitations that also point to directions for future research. First, the scale relies on two items per factor, which restricts both content coverage and reliability. Second, the design comprises only two waves and two school levels; additional waves and a broader age range are needed to trace developmental trajectories and to establish when the meaning students attach to meritocracy begins to shift. Third, and most consequentially, the lack of invariance across school cohorts indicates that meritocracy scales cannot be assumed to function equivalently across educational stages. Future studies should therefore examine differential item functioning, develop stage-sensitive item formulations, and adopt partial-invariance approaches [@putnick_measurement_2016; @vandeschoot_checklist_2012].  This would allow a more rigorous examination of group differences, such as the gender differences in meritocratic beliefs suggested by @gogescu_meritocracy_2025 and @khan_saying_2013, and of how beliefs about merit and privilege relate to the school outcomes for which they are likely to matter most: students' sense of justice and fairness, civic attitudes and engagement, perceptions of school climate, wellbeing, and academic motivation.
